analysis.one_liner: Doubles the time regulators have to sue negligent or fraudulent failed-bank officials.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with no cosponsors in June 1992, it was referred to a House Banking subcommittee and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: During the savings-and-loan crisis, federal regulators took over hundreds of failed banks and thrifts but often ran out of time to sue the officers, directors, and professionals whose negligence or fraud caused the failures. This bill would have doubled the window for those lawsuits from three years to six years, and let regulators revive claims that were about to expire when a receiver was appointed. Its stated goal was to recover billions of dollars for the deposit insurance funds, which are backstopped by taxpayers. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and the federal deposit insurance funds, which pay depositors when a bank fails and could have sued negligent or fraudulent bank officials for a longer period to recover losses. Depositors benefit indirectly because stronger recoveries help keep the insurance funds solvent.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and the deposit insurance funds

how_it_helps.text: Extends from three years to six years the deadline for federal conservators and receivers to sue bank personnel for negligence or fraud, under both the Federal Deposit Insurance Act and the Federal Credit Union Act.

Lets a receiver bring a claim if the failed institution could have sued at any point in the six years before the receiver was appointed, even if the clock had already run out, so lawsuits are not lost simply because regulators were overwhelmed by the volume of failures.

The bill's findings state that the sheer number of failures prevented regulators from filing suit within existing deadlines, that expired statutes of limitations blocked recovery from wrongdoers, and that taxpayers and the insurance funds may be unable to recover billions of dollars as a result.

analysis.who_pays: Officers, directors, and professional advisors of failed depository institutions, along with their liability insurers, who would face six years instead of three of legal exposure, including retroactively for receiverships already in progress.

drawbacks.text: The preservation-of-claims provision applies retroactively, reviving claims even where a federal receiver had already been appointed before the bill passed, which raises fair-notice concerns for defendants who believed their legal exposure had ended.

A longer liability window increases the cost of director-and-officer liability insurance and could make it harder for institutions to recruit qualified directors and outside professionals, a cost that eventually flows through to bank customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential recovery for taxpayers and deposit insurance funds was potentially in the billions, according to the bill's own findings, against a cost concentrated on a small group of failed-institution insiders and their insurers. The main design weakness is retroactivity, which applies new rules to closed cases; a narrower version could have avoided that objection while keeping most of the recovery value.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Banking Committee and then a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Bruce Vento (D-MN) introduced the bill on June 16, 1992, with no cosponsors.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs.
On July 1, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions Supervision, Regulation and Insurance, where it stayed with no further action.
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died without ever being reported out of committee or voted on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Officers, directors, and professional advisors of failed depository institutions, and their liability insurers, are better off because the extended deadline never became law, since lawsuits the bill would have preserved expired on the three-year clock. Taxpayers and the deposit insurance funds lost whatever recoveries the longer window might have produced.

for.name: Rep. Bruce F. Vento
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the statute of limitations for lawsuits over failed banks and credit unions.

against.name: House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill beyond referring it to a subcommittee; no hearing or markup was held before the Congress ended.

against.name: Subcommittee on Financial Institutions Supervision, Regulation and Insurance
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 1, 1992, and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the bill had no cosponsors, so no partisan or bloc positions are visible in the record.

industries.industry: Bank and credit union officers, directors, and professional advisors
industries.note: The bill would have doubled to six years the window in which regulators could sue them for negligence or fraud at failed institutions, and revived claims already near expiry. Its interest in the bill ran directly against the taxpayers footing the deposit-insurance bill.

A longer and retroactive liability window would have increased claims and premiums for policies covering failed-institution insiders. Their cost savings under the status quo came at the expense of the insurance funds' recoveries.

industries.industry: Federal deposit insurance system (FDIC and credit union insurance funds)
industries.note: The funds would have gained a longer window to recover billions from wrongdoers, strengthening a system backstopped by taxpayers. This is the government side of the ledger rather than a private industry.
